Reveille is a signal — most commonly a short, brisk bugle call — sounded early in the morning to wake up soldiers and officially mark the start of the military day.

Think of it as the military's version of an alarm clock, except instead of a beeping phone, it's a musical signal blown on a bugle (a brass instrument), sometimes replaced by a drum roll or even a recorded tune played over loudspeakers. The moment reveille sounds, every soldier in the camp or base is expected to get up, get dressed, and begin the day.

Reveille is not just a sound — it's a formal daily military routine, almost like a small ceremony. Here is what typically unfolds:

  1. At a fixed time each morning (often as early as 5:00 or 6:00 AM), the bugler plays the reveille call.
  2. Soldiers must immediately rise from their bunks.
  3. In many armies, reveille is paired with a flag-raising ceremony — the national flag is hoisted as the call is played, and soldiers stand at attention to honor it.
  4. After reveille, the official activities of the military day begin — roll call, physical training, drills, and so on.

So reveille is not merely a sound. It is the symbolic and practical starting gun of a soldier's day.
What Does the Bugle Call Actually Sound Like?

The reveille bugle call is a specific, recognizable melody — short (about 20–30 seconds), lively, and rising in pitch. It has a "wake up, the day is here!" quality to it. If you've ever watched a war film set in a military camp, you've almost certainly heard it. It's one of the most iconic sounds in military culture worldwide.
How Is It Used in a Sentence?

• "The soldiers were jolted awake by the sharp sound of reveille at 5 AM."
  • "The bugler sounded reveille as the flag was raised over the base."
  • "There was no sleeping in — reveille came every morning without fail."

Notice that you often say "sound reveille" (a bugler sounds reveille) or "hear reveille." You don't usually say "play reveille" or "ring reveille," though "sound reveille" is the most standard phrasing.
Is It Used Outside the Military?

Yes, though rarely. Writers and speakers sometimes use reveille figuratively — as a poetic or dramatic way of saying "a wake-up call" or "a signal that something new is beginning."

For example:

  • "The economic crisis served as a reveille for governments around the world." (meaning: it jolted them awake to a new reality)
  • "Spring feels like nature's own reveille." (meaning: a signal that the world is waking up after winter)

This figurative use is less common and more literary in flavor. In everyday speech, you will almost always encounter "reveille" in a military context.

To fully understand reveille, it helps to know its opposite: taps. While reveille signals the beginning of the military day (wake up), taps is the bugle call sounded at night to signal lights-out (time to sleep). Taps is also played at military funerals. Together, reveille and taps bookend the military day — one opens it, the other closes it.

Reveille, in short, is the sound that tells a soldier: "The day has begun. Rise."
